statement: If a treatment has a strictly higher success rate than the alternative within every stratum of a population - P(S | T, C) > P(S | not-T, C) and P(S | T, not-C) > P(S | not-T, not-C) - then it has a strictly higher overall success rate, P(S | T) > P(S | not-T).
definitions: S, T, C are events on a finite probability space; all four events (T and C), (T and not-C), (not-T and C), (not-T and not-C) have positive probability so every conditional probability is defined.
ground_truth_witness: Take 200 equally likely individuals. In stratum C (easy cases) the treatment T is given to 10 people with 9 successes (rate 9/10) and the alternative to 90 people with 72 successes (rate 4/5). In stratum not-C (hard cases) T is given to 90 people with 27 successes (rate 3/10) and the alternative to 10 people with 2 successes (rate 1/5). T is strictly better inside each stratum (9/10 > 4/5 and 3/10 > 1/5), yet overall T succeeds on 36 of its 100 cases and the alternative on 74 of its 100, so P(S|T) = 9/25 < 37/50 = P(S|not-T): the aggregate comparison reverses because T is applied mostly to hard cases.
reference_authority: published counterexample (book-cited), verified per partB_feasibility records
book_citation: J. M. Stoyanov, Counterexamples in Probability, Wiley, 1987 (3rd ed., Dover, 2013); Chapter 1 material on conditional probabilities (Simpson-type reversal of conditional inequalities under aggregation); example number not pinned from freely available sources.
